question: Where do you aim when giving a subcutaneous injection?

options.A: Deep inside the main skeletal muscle tissue
options.C: Into the layer of fat beneath the skin
options.D: Between the outer epidermis and the dermis

explanation: You've got this! Subcutaneous simply means 'under the skin,' targeting the fatty layer right beneath the dermis. Great job remembering your tissue layers!

question: Why does a subcutaneous injection take longer to work than an IV injection?

options.A: Injected drugs must travel through the liver first
options.B: Skin layers create a physical barrier to fluid movement
options.C: Subcutaneous fat actively destroys active drug molecules
options.D: Subcutaneous tissue has a limited blood supply

explanation: Think of it this way: fatty tissue has fewer blood vessels compared to veins, so it takes a little longer for the medicine to hitch a ride into your bloodstream!

question: What is the usual maximum safe volume of fluid for one subcutaneous injection in an adult?

options.A: Any volume ordered by the doctor

explanation: Keeping subcutaneous volumes small (under 1.5 mL) keeps the patient comfortable and prevents painful swelling in that little pocket of fat.

question: A doctor prescribes 3.0 mL of medication to be given subcutaneously. What should you do?

options.A: Split the dose and inject it into two different subcutaneous sites
options.B: Administer the full dose as a single subcutaneous injection
options.C: Call the doctor to question the volume and discuss alternative routes
options.D: Give the entire medication into the deltoid muscle instead

explanation: Spot on! 3.0 mL is way too much for one sub-Q site and would cause unnecessary pain and tissue damage. Always speak up and clarify with the prescriber.

question: Which needle gauge is best for a routine subcutaneous injection?
explanation: Higher gauge numbers mean thinner needles! A 25 to 30 gauge needle slips in smoothly and keeps the injection as painless as possible.

question: Why do nurses pinch the skin when giving a subcutaneous injection to a slim patient?

options.A: To squeeze out trapped air bubbles inside the syringe
options.B: To speed up the absorption of the medication into blood
options.C: To lift the fatty tissue away from the underlying muscle
options.D: To numb the nerve endings near the injection site

explanation: Pinching gathers up that cozy layer of fat and safely lifts it away from the muscle underneath, ensuring your needle goes exactly where it's supposed to.

question: Where is the favorite spot for patients to self-inject insulin regularly?

options.A: The chest wall over the sternum
options.B: The abdomen, avoiding the navel area
options.C: The anterior lower leg near the shin
options.D: The inner surface of the forearm

explanation: The tummy is easy to reach and has a nice, reliable layer of fat that absorbs insulin smoothly. Just remember to stay clear of the belly button!

question: Why must patients constantly rotate their injection sites?

options.A: To reduce the financial cost of purchasing new syringes
options.B: To prevent localized skin hardening and altered drug absorption
options.C: To stop the needle from becoming dull during repeated use
options.D: To ensure the medication reaches the bloodstream much faster

explanation: Using the exact same spot over and over can cause fatty lumps (lipohypertrophy) and mess up how the drug is absorbed. Moving around keeps the skin healthy!

question: Why must you wait for the alcohol on the skin to dry before sticking the patient?

options.A: To activate the antiseptic properties of the alcohol
options.B: To ensure the skin surface becomes completely sterile
options.C: To make the outer skin layers easier to pierce
options.D: To prevent stinging and burning sensations upon entry

explanation: Patience pays off! If the alcohol isn't dry, the needle drags it down into the tissue, causing a sharp, unnecessary sting for your patient.

question: What is the very first thing you do right after pulling the needle out of a patient?

options.A: Activate the needle safety device and drop it into a sharps container
options.B: Recap the needle immediately using both hands for safety
options.C: Massage the injection site vigorously to speed up absorption
options.D: Wipe the skin again with a fresh alcohol swab to clean any blood

explanation: Safety first! Always pop the safety on and drop the used needle straight into the sharps box to protect yourself and others from accidental pricks.

question: Why don't we pull back (aspirate) on the plunger anymore for routine subcutaneous shots like insulin?

options.A: It makes the medication completely inactive in the syringe
options.B: It increases the risk of the needle breaking in the skin
options.C: It causes unnecessary tissue trauma and increases bruising
options.D: It causes the plunger to stick permanently inside the barrel

explanation: Modern practice shows that the chance of hitting a vessel here is tiny. Pulling back just causes extra discomfort and bruising for no real benefit.

question: Which of these is NOT a typical local issue at a subcutaneous injection site?
explanation: You've got this! Anaphylaxis is a full-body allergic reaction, not just a local problem happening right at the patch of skin where the injection went in.

question: What is the absolute best way to check if a patient is ready to give their own shots at home?

options.A: Ask a family member to take full responsibility for the task
options.B: Provide a written multiple-choice test on injection theory
options.C: Have the patient perform a return demonstration of the steps
options.D: Ask the patient to read the medication package insert aloud

explanation: Seeing is believing! Having them show you how they do it lets you coach them, build their confidence, and make sure they are doing it safely.

question: Which injection site symptom means the patient needs to call a doctor right away?

options.A: A small pinprick dot of dry blood on the skin surface
options.B: Pus drainage, severe pain, and spreading warmth
options.C: Temporary slight coolness where the alcohol dried
options.D: Mild fading skin discoloration from a tiny bruise

explanation: Those are classic red flags for an infection! Pus, severe pain, and warmth mean the site needs medical attention quickly.
